utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case IT-09-92-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could I have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Dermot Groome. I am here with Peter McCloskey, Roeland Bos and Janet Stewart for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Branko Lukic accompanied by Mr. Milos Saljic, Milenko Dundjer and Nenad Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. And I see Mr. Mladic is present as well. This is the seventh Status Conference in this case, and as with the previous Status Conferences, any guidance or any decisions that will be announced, they have been deliberated and adopted by the Chamber as a whole. The purpose of this, as it was for all the other Status Conferences, is to monitor the progress made with regard to pre-trial work and preparing for trial. Earlier this week I presided over a Rule 65 ter meeting with the parties during which we discussed certain pre-trial matters in more detail than this Status Conference is -- conference allows for. I move to the first subject which is pre-trial planning and preparation for trial. On the 9th of March of this year, the Defence filed a motion requesting a time and word limit extension for its pre-trial brief. On the 12th of March, the Prosecution responded and did not oppose the request. On the 14th of March, through an informal communication, the Trial Chamber granted a time extension for the filing of the Defence pre-trial brief until the 3rd of April, 2012, and a word limit extension to 20.000 words, and that decision is hereby put on the record. In light of its decision to grant the time extension for the filing of the Defence pre-trial brief, the Chamber now announces several new deadlines. First, pursuant to Rule 65 ter (F) and Rule 73 bis, the previously set date for the Pre-Trial Conference, which was the 17th of April of 2012, must be adjusted to provide for a three-week interval between it and the filing of the Defence pre-trial brief. The Pre-Trial Conference will therefore be held on the 24th of April of 2012 at 9.00 a.m. Second, at the 6th of October Status Conference, the Chamber set the deadline for the Prosecution to complete its Rule 68(i) disclosure in relation to the Defence pre-trial brief at 30 days from the filing of that brief. As the pre-trial brief is now due on the 3rd of April, the Prosecution's Rule 68(i) disclosure in relation to this filing is accordingly moved to the 3rd of May. Further, as the Pre-Trial Conference has been moved back a week, the Chamber considers that it would be helpful to schedule a final Rule 65 ter meeting to discuss any outstanding issue with the parties. The Chamber therefore informs the parties that a Rule 65 ter meeting is now scheduled for the 17th of April, the exact time to be communicated at a later date by the Registry. In relation to this meeting, the Prosecution is instructed to file a final pre-trial report by the 11th of April. Given the shorter than usual period of time between Rule 65 ter meetings, the pre-trial report need only address those issues that require ongoing updates or where there have been new developments since the last report. Have the parties any questions in relation to the scheduling issues I raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for asking you at this moment regarding this Scheduling Order, but is it possible to make closer this 65 ter meeting scheduled for 17th of April and Status Conference on the 24th? It would be easier for us to have only shorter window since we have to be here and work on the case and go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean the 65 ter meeting closer to the Pre-Trial Conference, not a week in between but closer to the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that, Mr. Lukic. Of course, you'll understand that we have to look at many things like the Judges' agenda as the availability of courtroom, interpreter. I mean, we have to consider it, but before we do so, Mr. Groome, would you have any concern in making it later than the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We'll be available whenever the Chamber sets a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- Mr. Lukic, I do understand that you want to shorten the window of your presence here in The Hague. Now, the 24th is a Tuesday. Would it meet major objections if we still would have it before that weekend?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whatever you can make on this issue, Your Honour. It would be better if it's Monday so we have -- can be here for only two, three days, but if necessary, we can be here on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may understand that of course the Chamber needs some time in between as well. I mean, it's not that we can deal with all those matters without sufficient time in between to -- to further prepare for the next step. But I'll consider it and -- together with my colleagues and we'll let you know as soon as possible, even if this would be through an informal communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then any or matter in relation to these scheduling issues? If not, I'll continue. On the 23rd of February, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to file a corrigendum to its Rule 65 ter (E) filings by the 2nd of March, 2012. On the 2nd of March, the Prosecution filed the corrigendum which contained corrections to its witness list, the reference tables and its exhibit list. In relation to the exhibit list, the corrigendum states and I quote: "The Prosecution has identified exhibits which were inadvertently not included on the exhibit list." Annex C to the exhibit list contains 123 additional exhibits the Prosecution seeks to add to the exhibit list. Mr. Groome, the Chamber finds that a corrigendum filing is not the correct matter in which to add exhibits to the exhibit list. In the interests of expeditiousness, the Chamber has decided to interpret the corrigendum as a Prosecution request for leave to add these 123 exhibits to its Rule 65 ter (E) exhibit list, and the Defence therefore is instructed to file a response to the request within two weeks from today. Any comments on what I just said? Also perhaps, Mr. Groome, on how we interpreted your corrigendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that that is a reasonable interpretation, and if the Chamber so wishes, the Prosecution would be prepared to make more detailed submissions explaining why those documents were not on the original list that was filed in early, mid-February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see what objections will be raised and if they are such that the Prosecution would consider that it would have a better explanation to rebut those objections which it did not give because it considered the filing just the corrigendum in which it was free to add to the exhibit list, then we'll see how to proceed and whether we give you an opportunity perhaps if you request for such an opportunity to further explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further comments from the Defence, I see. Now, as was set out in the Scheduling Order, the trial in this case will begin on the 14th of May, 2012, with the Prosecution's opening statement. The Chamber now sets the deadline for the Prosecution to inform the Chamber of the amount of time it will need for its opening statement to the 20th of April. As agreed in this Monday's Rule 65 ter meeting, this same date, April the 20th, is also the new deadline for the Defence to notify the Chamber if it will also make an opening statement and whether Mr. Mladic wishes to make a statement before the presentation of the Prosecution's case. That notification was to include the amount of time required for any such statements. At last month's 65 ter meeting and Status Conference, the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter (E) filings were discussed in relation to the amount of estimated time for its Rule 92 ter viva voce and expert witnesses. At the 23rd of February Status Conference, the Prosecution was reminded of the Chamber's 10th of November, 2011, guidance, in which the Chamber limited the time for examination-in-chief of Rule 92 ter witnesses to 30 minutes, to be increased only exceptionally and with the Chamber's leave after a showing of good cause for a specific witness. For Rule 92 ter witnesses, the Prosecution's average estimated time is one hour, which includes the time required for the attestation in court, reading of the witness's statement summary, and the examination-in-chief. While I stress that nothing is carved in stone yet, the Chamber now provides the parties with its general assumptions as to the amount of time for cross-examination of witnesses. For the cross-examination of such Rule 92 ter witnesses, the Chamber assumes an average time for cross-examination of 2.5 hours. This number is, of course, dependent on the volume of the documents introduced through the witness and the overall scope of the 92 ter materials. For the cross-examination of viva voce witnesses, the Chamber estimates the time needed for cross-examination to be approximately 60 per cent of the time used for examination-in-chief. In the interests of a fair and expeditious trial, the Chamber will monitor the conduct of examination-in-chief, cross-examination, as well as any re-examination. And further, the parties should keep these time estimates in mind, and if already anticipating deviations from them, the parties should indicate this to the Chamber no later than two weeks before the expected start of the witness's testimony. For Rule 94 bis witnesses, Mr. Lukic, the Chamber requests that you indicate the estimated cross-examination time in the respective Defence notices under Rule 94 bis to the extent possible, of course, at this time. However, you may also file revised estimates for these expert witnesses, again, no later than two weeks before the expected start of their testimony. As you have already filed your notices for proposed experts Philipps and Butler, please provide the estimated cross-examination time two weeks before their testimony should they indeed be called. And I immediately add to this, Mr. Lukic, that this is not in any way an indication of the Chamber's position in relation to your objections to these two witnesses and their proposed expert reports. We are still considering those but do not think that we should refrain from already preparing for practicalities in case we might not honour your objections. At the Rule 65 ter meeting, the parties discussed the Prosecution's expected witness order for the first part of the trial, which is to say until the summer recess. The Chamber hereby instructs the Prosecution to notify the Chamber and the Defence of its expected witness order until the summer recess by April the 13th, 2012. In relation to that notification, at the 65 ter meeting the parties also discussed the Prosecution's 65 ter (E) (i) and (iii) submissions which will address any admissions by the parties and information about whether the authenticity of exhibits is challenged by the Defence. Mr. Groome, at the 65 ter meeting you proposed linking discussions with the Defence on these matters to the Prosecution's publication of its order of witnesses. The Chamber therefore instructs the Prosecution to make its first Rule 65 ter (E)(i) and (iii) submissions by the 27th of April. This will give the parties time to discuss possible agreement on the exhibits the Prosecution seeks to tender through those witnesses who are expected to be called in the first part of the trial and also discuss -- to discuss any admissions in relation to those witnesses' expected testimony. So it's the first submissions, the submissions which of course are now detached from the pre-trial brief but are in the Rules described in the same paragraph should deal with the first batch of witnesses until the summer recess. Any comments or any questions in relation to the matters I just raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one issue that I would like to raise with the Chamber. The Chamber again has reaffirmed its directive that the Prosecution with respect to 92 ter witnesses would be limited to 30 minutes. When the Prosecution developed its presentation of evidence for this case, it considered that many of the witnesses that it will call to the witness stand have an abundance of evidence that is directly relevant to this case. Some of these witnesses were internationals who spent several years in the region and have many observations and much evidence to provide the Chamber. When the Prosecution developed its witness list, it considered that while these witnesses could be called viva voce, doing so would require days of evidence, of leading their evidence, and we used as an indication of how long their evidence would take to lead live prior cases in which they have testified in which the evidence took that long. The Prosecution considered that 92 ter was an appropriate mechanism to use to allow the witnesses to provide the evidence directly relevant to Mr. Mladic, meetings they had with Mr. Mladic or direct observations they made of Mr. Mladic as well as other members of the joint criminal enterprise, but yet allow the more efficient entry into evidence of the bulk of the remainder of their evidence in written form. The Chamber's directive seems to preclude that possibility, and the Prosecution would appreciate the Chamber explaining the rationale for that and it may require the Prosecution to revisit whether or not it can call these witnesses 92 ter, and I think it would most certainly result in an additional time being needed to lead that evidence viva voce. I think that would be unfortunate, because I think there is a very efficient way of allowing a witness with such an abundance of evidence to provide it in a way that is useful to the Chamber, can be fully cross-examined by the Defence and significantly reduce the time that's spent in court leading that evidence. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll consider this with -- together with my colleagues. When we decided to allow for 30 minutes examination-in-chief, we have considered the practice in many Chambers in this Tribunal, and we have balanced, of course, the advantages of hearing viva voce evidence and to read evidence from statements. It is a rather complex matter. I'll again discuss it with my colleagues on the basis of the submissions you just made, and then we'll give it the appropriate follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It would also be helpful for the Prosecution to know precisely what the Chamber means when it says "good cause." Traditionally the only test of admission into evidence has been relevance. Now this new concept of good cause as applied to decision such as this, it is an unknown or relatively unknown concept in the jurisprudence, and it would be very helpful for the Prosecution to be able to have a better understanding of what the Chamber considers what might, for example, be good cause that we could better plan our -- the present of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll include this in the follow-up. I promised we would give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. What the Defence would like you to reconsider is the right for our cross-examination of viva voce witnesses, although we have only seven, I think, at this moment, but usually in previous trials when I -- where I took part we had the equal amount for cross-examination as the Prosecution had in their direct examination. So if possible, I'll kindly ask Your Honours to reconsider and give us the same amount of time as the Prosecution has for their chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have -- Mr. Lukic, we have determined the 60 per cent on the basis of quite a variety of practices before various Trial Chambers, including issues like is there one accused or are there more accused in that case, what time was granted and what time was used. So we did quite a bit of statistical analysis. So therefore, if you would wish to give further information on the -- I would say the basis you refer to other cases where you say it was a hundred per cent, I know of other cases which used a hundred per cent. I also know of other cases which used 60 per cent. I know of cases where 105 or 110 per cent was used with three cues. So we did quite some research. If you would like to add any data or if you would like to add any arguments why 60 per cent would not be sufficient, you're invited to file that as -- or to communicate that to the Chamber most likely in a filing as quickly as possible so that we, when considering your request, that we have all relevant information available. And, of course, as the Prosecution would have any specific information which would assist the Chamber in deciding whether or not to grant an extension of time which would be 66 per cent of what we had on our mind, yes, now, because from 60 to a hundred, that is two-thirds to be added, 66 per cent. If the Prosecution has any such information, it's also invited to -- to inform the Chamber, because when we're talking about cross-examination, we're not only talking about cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses but Defence but also about cross-examination of Defence witnesses if they'll ever be called, if there will be a Defence case, cross-examination by the Prosecution. Could we say that if you have any further thoughts to be brought to the Chamber's attention that we'd like to see them within a week from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Can I simply say that while I appreciate that time limits are an essential part of the work that we do here, I think the best practice has always been the Judges sitting at the trial making informed decisions about what the time that was necessary for a full exploration of the witness's evidence and so the Prosecution would never oppose any reasonable request for time to do that and defer to the Chamber in what precise amount of time would be necessary to have such an exploration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When I say 60 per cent of the time, I would like to refer to what I said earlier, is that these are general assumptions we are considering at this moment, which are not yet carved in stone. And in relation to the 92 ter witnesses, I already indicated that it would, of course, also depend on the volume of the documents and through the overall scope of the Rule 92 ter materials. Whatever our guidance will be in terms of numbers or percentages, the Chamber will, and that was the next thing, I would say, is that we'll closely monitor the way in which both examination-in-chief and cross-examination or re-examination is conducted. If that is very efficient, to the point, and focused, and if it's clear that more time would be needed, then of course we'll seriously consider that, because -- but what we're doing here is for planning purposes, for scheduling purposes, to try to find a basis on which we can work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if I can address one more issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding 92 ter witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that this time-frame for cross-examination is having in mind limited number of documents the Prosecution can introduce through that witness, and we hope that if there are more documents introduced that we'll have the extent of time for cross-examination for that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the number of documents to be used also depends on how we are going to deal with bar table motions and what documents will be introduced directly through witnesses, which is of course the preferred way of receiving documents. I think I hinted already at that when I said that the number is, of course, dependent on the volume of documents introduced through the witness and the overall scope of the Rule 92 ter materials that alluded already to the matter you apparently wanted to bring to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move on. At the 23rd of February Status Conference, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to refile its Rule 92 bis motion in relation to Witness RM057 by the 2nd of March. On the 2nd of March, the Prosecution re-filed the motion, requesting provisional acceptance of the unsigned statement until the Prosecution is able to secure the witness's declaration. On the 16th of March, the Defence filed its response opposing the motion and requesting an extension of the word limit for its response. The request to exceed the word limit was granted by the Chamber through an informal communication on the 21st of March, and that decision is hereby put on the record. On the 23rd of March, the Prosecution filed an a motion request leave to reply to the Defence's response. The Chamber hereby grants the request for leave to reply. In relation to this same motion, in its response, the Defence objected to the general practice of provisionally admitting unsigned statements until a declaration can be obtained. In relation to provisional acceptance of Rule 92 bis witness statements without the witness's declaration as a general practice, the Chamber informs the parties that this will be addressed in the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's motion. We'll deal with that then. On the 17th of February, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting the admission of evidence of a witness pursuant to Rule 92 quater and submitted an annotated transcript which indicated those portions of the transcript upon which the Prosecution plans to rely. The Prosecution also proposed a similar procedure for future Rule 92 quater motions. At the 23rd of February Status Conference in relation to Rule 92 quater motions, the Chamber informed the parties that for future motions the Prosecution should not tender entire transcripts or prior testimony with annotations but only tender those portions upon it will -- upon which it will rely. On the 15th of March, 2012, the Defence filed its response. On the 22nd of March, the Prosecution filed a motion seeking leave to reply to the Defence response, and the Chamber hereby grants the request for leave to reply. Further, in its response, the Defence stated that it opposes the transcript annotation procedure suggested by the Prosecution as well as the Chamber's subsequent guidance to the parties for future Rule 92 quater motions. The Chamber informs the parties that the Chamber will address this issue, including the Defence's objections to its guidance, in its decision on the motion. Mr. Groome, if you would not mind, I would like to deal with the -- no. You apparently want to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I rose simply to inform the Chamber that the Prosecution is in the process of finalising a detailed submission on some of the guidance that the Chamber has provided and some of the potential problems that the Prosecution believes exists in that guidance. We expect to file that on Monday. I just wanted to let the Chamber know that that was coming in the event that it wanted to receive that before it finalised its decision on this matter, and this is one of the issues that we do make submissions regarding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is that -- would that be part of the reply you asked leave for or would it be a separate submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have put together or we are finalising a comprehensive submission in which we believe some of the guidance the Chamber has given with respect to 92 bis, ter, quater, the number of exhibits, the bar table motions cause conflict and when considered together creates some problems that the Prosecution wants to bring to the Chamber's attention. So it does deal in part with this. Some of these issues may also be touched upon in the reply. The focus of this -- the -- the -- this submission is the interaction of the different guidances provided by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It may well be then if it's an extensive submission that the Defence would like to make further submissions on the matter. Let's first wait and see what we receive on Monday, and we know that apart from the usual responses and replies there will be a submission which deals with several matters relevant for some of the pending motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I return to the response by the Defence on the motion we just dealt with. In that response, the Defence requested that should the Prosecution motion be granted, that it then be permitted to make a submission on those portions of the transcript it would also wanted admitted. This was also discussed at the Rule 65 ter meeting and the Chamber now puts on the record that the Defence has until the 5th of April to file a submission identifying those portions of the transcript it would like to have added if the motion would be granted. This instruction again, Mr. Lukic, is not to be understood as in any way to anticipate on the decision the Chamber will give, but it's mainly given for very practical reasons, so that we don't lose time at a later stage if a decision on the motion would be A or B. Then finally, Mr. Groome, at the Rule 65 ter meeting you stated that you would clarify the issue of the missing curriculum vitae by today. However, this matter is, as we see, also addressed in your reply. As the request for leave to reply and reply were filed together and before the Rule 65 ter meeting, does the Prosecution have any further, any additional information it would like to put on the record in relation to this issue other than what is already contained in your reply? Now, I do understand in the reply you mainly refer to having disclosed the CV, which of course is not exactly the same as having that same CV attached to a motion. I just make this observation before I give you an opportunity to further address the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The only additional piece of information I would wish to provide the Chamber is that in light of the fact that Lukic -- Mr. Lukic has been unable to find the copy of the document in a prior disclosure, we have re-disclosed it today to him. So Mr. Lukic now has possession of another copy of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, for the Chamber, of course, it is important that we have a CV attached to a motion if it's relevant to that, because whatever you disclose to Mr. Lukic is not necessarily then known to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will file a supplement to our reply with permission of the Court that attaches that document, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether we call it a supplement or corrigendum, but at least so we have received that CV -- we have received that in relation to the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, having heard that whether re-disclosed or disclosed for the third time that you have available the CV, the Chamber would like to receive any further comments on that CV by the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the Prosecution has provided us with the missing CV by way of e-mail on 27th of March, 2012, and the Defence does not intend to make any additional submissions relatively to the Rule 92 quater motion arising out of the CV. The arguments as presented in our responsive filing of 15th of March, 2012, remain valid and we continue to stand on those submissions and seek the relief identified therein. As permitting, this witness's testimony via Rule 92 quater would unfairly prejudice the rights of Mr. Mladic to confront the evidence against him and have a fair and due process. Just because Mr. Mladic is among the last accused at the dock does not mean that his rights should be abridged or that he should not have at least the same fair chance that prior accused had to confront the evidence against them. That's all we have on this issue, Your Honour, and we are not going to file anything additional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I gave this time limit because earlier you said, We can't comment on the CV because we haven't got it. Now, that apparently you have received it. You do not feel any need to further comment on the CV but your objections against admission pending and are the same, and you have underlined them a minute ago with some further submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider that in deciding the motion. The -- at the 23rd of February Status Conference, the Prosecution raised concerns in relation to the Chamber's guidance on associated exhibit limitations and made a proposal regarding bar table submissions. I alluded to that earlier already. The Prosecution proposed that it be entitled to submit a bar table motion at the conclusion of each individual component of its case rather than near the end of its case presentation in its entirety. The Defence stated that it has no objections to the current guidance and suggested no changes, and the Chamber has informed the parties that it would consider their proposals. The Chamber has considered it and even reached a conclusion, Mr. Groome, but the question which now arises is whether it would be wiser for the Chamber to wait for your submissions of next Monday before I give you what we thought to be the appropriate solution, having heard the submissions until this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, our submissions planned for Monday do not include the timing of bar table motions and would have no impact on the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I can proceed. After having considered the suggestions and submissions by Prosecution and Defence, the Chamber informs the Prosecution that its proposal to submit bar table motions at the close of its presentation related to individual components of its case is acceptable as long as the motion fully complies with the Chamber's already-announced guidance on bar table submissions. In that regard, and to some extent I perhaps revisit that matter slightly, in that regard I remind the parties of that guidance in which the Chamber stated, and I quote: "Any bar table submission should be filed at a late stage of each party's case when it is clear to the tendering party that the relevant documents were not and could not have been tendered through any witness." Of course, where I said the late stage of the party's case has now to be understood at -- at the close of the presentation related to individual components of the case. In this same respect I also remind the parties of the Chamber's stated preference to have documentary evidence tendered in court through witnesses who can provide the proper contextualisation. To the extent the Prosecution can demonstrate that a specific component of its case is coming to a close and that the documents could not have been tendered through any witness, the Chamber will consider the Prosecution's bar table submissions. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the Chamber uses the phrase "could not have been tendered through any witness," does that include the Chamber's guidance setting the -- the limit of five exhibits with respect to the admission of exhibits with respect to witnesses, particularly, I think, 92 bis witnesses? The Chamber had set a limit such as five exhibits. Would that be incorporated into the concept of "could not have included"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that may play a role. I'll further discuss this with my colleagues, but could not, of course, we have to make a difference between viva voce witness where such a limit does not apply, 92 ter witnesses, 92 bis material. We will consider and give you further guidance on what should be understood by "could not." It could also be that -- there are of course many factors such as none of the witnesses called could be used to introduce this document, although it is related to the subject matter of that witness, but he might not be aware of that document in any case. So I think there are -- there may be a variety of circumstances, and we'll consider whether the one you just mentioned would be one of them, a variety of circumstances which might lead to the conclusion that a document could not be introduced through a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber notes that on the 19th of March, the Prosecution filed a motion seeking a word limit extension for its upcoming submissions on the presentation and tendering of evidence. Perhaps a small question, Mr. Groome. That is -- that is the same or not the same of what we could expect on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is the same motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the same motion. Yes. Yes. You say motion. It was a motion seeking to extend the word limit for what you called a submission, not necessarily a motion. I also understood that what we can expect on Monday is a submission rather than a motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we will be seeking relief, and the relief that we will be seeking is to have a detailed hearing with all the parties present to discuss some of these issues. The Prosecution takes the position that it is time very well spent to flesh out all of the issues related to how the Prosecution and the Defence will present their case prior to the start of the trial. We believe that it will result in a more efficient trial. It will result in a body of evidence that will put the Chamber in the best position to adjudicate this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you may have noticed, the Chamber also wants to clarify many procedural issues before the start of the trial. At the same time, the Chamber wants to avoid that we enter into a rigid system where we have no -- no manoeuvring space anymore. So we have to try to find a balance then. That's clear, Mr. -- the -- I started with the motion you filed seeking a word limit extension. On the 21st of March, two days after this motion was filed, the Chamber informed the Prosecution through an informal communication that the request for a word limit extension was denied, and that decision is hereby put on the record. Now, in light of the upcoming written submissions from the Prosecution, the Chamber will not make any more statements at this moment on the matters raised in this context at the last Status Conference until it has received the party's written submissions. Finally, I'd like to remind the parties that at the 23rd of February Status Conference, the Chamber set the deadline for the submission of the agreed facts progress report to the 27th of April, 2012, and from that date onwards on the last working day of every other subsequent month. As a clarification for the parties, there's no need to submit a joint agreed facts progress report before the April Rule 65 ter meeting. I move on to the Rule 73 bis (C) decision. On the 19th of March, the Chamber staff sent an e-mail to the parties listing certain questions to be discussed at Monday's Rule 65 ter meeting in relation to its upcoming Rule 73 bis (C) decision. For those in the audience and following these proceedings from outside the courtroom, I'll briefly explain that Rule 73 bis (C) provides that after having heard from the Prosecution, the Chamber shall determine the number of witnesses the Prosecution may call and the time available to the Prosecution for presenting its evidence. At the Rule 65 ter meeting, the Prosecution made its submissions, which I now briefly will review. The first issue discussed was in relation to why certain witnesses were proposed as Rule 92 ter witnesses as opposed to Rule 92 bis witnesses. The Prosecution stated that it intended to give consideration to the Chamber's view that perhaps these witnesses could be dealt with through Rule 92 bis. However, the Prosecution also informed the Chamber that a number of the listed witnesses are testifying in relation to crime base incidents and often are the sole remaining survivors of these incidents. The second issue discussed was in relation to the purpose of calling Prosecution investigators primarily to explain and evaluate documentary evidence. The Prosecution submitted that these witnesses would be necessary in case that the Defence challenges certain evidence, mainly dealing with videos and books compiled by the Prosecution staff. These witnesses would, if needed, testify to the chain of custody of the original materials and the manner in which these materials were assembled into the aforementioned videos and books. Finally, the third issue discussed was in relation to the number of witnesses listed to give evidence on intercept communications and Count 11 of the indictment, the UN hostage issue. In relation to the intercept communications, the Prosecution clarified its intention to call a few supervisors of the intercept records and that it will only proceed to call the remainder of the intercept operators if it believes it necessary to meet its burden of proof. In relation to the UN hostages, the Prosecution recalled that its pre-trial brief sets out over 200 hostages in various locations. Accordingly, the Prosecution has proposed four hours of court time for the more central witnesses, but will then rely on Rule 92 bis statements for 11 additional witnesses to establish all the hostage situations at the different locations. Have the parties any questions or any comments related to the Prosecution's Rule 73 bis (C) submissions? Mr. Groome, if you would start.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The only other observation or submission I would make, Your Honour, that occurred to me after our meeting earlier this week that -- for example, that for the documents that the Prosecution investigators were likely to deal with in their evidence and likely the same with respect to intercept evidence, that the Chamber might want to consider the benefit of allowing exceptionally in those circumstances the Prosecution to file a bar table motion seeking admission of such documents. And at the beginning of the commencement of that part of the case if that issue could be litigated, as it were, in paper, if the Prosecution received a decision in which it believe it was no longer necessary to call those witnesses, the Prosecution would then proceed to remove those witnesses from the witness list. So there maybe some advantage, at least in that case, of reversing the order of when bar table motions can be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this perhaps adds another category to documents that could not be introduced through witnesses. They could, but preferably would not be introduced through witnesses. That's then a kind of separate situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you want to raise any matter, do you have any comments, or already respond on what the Prosecution raised? I would imagine you would need more time to prepare, but please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would like time to address the issue, and only as I mentioned in our 65 ter meeting on Monday, the Defence is never in favour of 22 [sic] bis statements unless it has the chance to cross-examine the witness. So probably it will be something that we'll have to address at a later stage and in light of your guidance that we should provide how much time we need for any 92 bis witness if allowed to cross-examine them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although, of course, we were primarily interested in 92 ter. But if you say if we do not accept this witness to be a 92 bis witness, then at least to tell us what time estimate you would have for cross-examination you consider necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you would not mind looking at the transcript that I add 70 to the 22 bis so that we are on 92 bis. Yes. Mathematics has always been one of my favourites. So 70 is added there to the 22 bis witnesses. Any further matter in relation to this? Perhaps I should add one word. To the extent you have -- you may have understood the questions by the Chamber, Mr. Groome, as questions steering matters in any way, that's not what the Chamber tried to do. Sometimes raising questions cause the respondent to think over again what apparently the one who put the question considered worth of being thought of or again. The Chamber, of course, is not telling any of the parties how it should present its case, although, of course, it is still supervising the presentation of evidence in a general sense under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecutor appreciates that that's what the Chamber intended, and the Prosecution always stands ready to provide any information the Chamber wishes regarding the presentation of its case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. We move on. Next item, disclosure. On the 20th of February, 2012, at the sixth 65 ter meeting, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to include in its recertification notice of compliance with respect to Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure any resolution of the concerns raised by the Defence in its correspondence of the 12th of February related to potential noncompliance with Rule 66(A)(ii). On the 23rd of February, 2012, at the sixth Status Conference, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to file this recertification notice on the 12th of March of 2012, but to date, no filing has been made. At this past Monday's Rule 65 ter meeting, the Prosecution explained that its Rule 66(A)(ii) review is linked to its Rule 68(i) review for which it had received an extension until the 2nd of April, and which it thought applied also to the Rule 66(A)(ii) recertification notice. The Chamber accepts the Prosecution's position in relation to the recertification notice, and this filing may be made on the 2nd of April. However, in relation to addressing the Defence concerns raised on the 12th of February at the Rule 65 ter meeting, you suggested, Mr. Groome, that you would first attempt to resolve this by today's Status Conference. Therefore, is there anything you would like to report at this moment as to the resolution of this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution has had several productive meetings this week with the Mladic Defence team. With respect to the disclosure of prior statements of witnesses, Rule 66(A)(ii) material, the Prosecution has worked with the Mladic Defence to identify missing materials, and Mr. Lukic was in fact correct in noting the absence of the disclosure of some of these documents. They are primarily translations of documents that had been provided. They number in total approximately 900 documents. Today we have processed those -- approximately 75 per cent of those documents and have disclosed them today. For technical reasons there remain 25 per cent of those documents still to be processed. That is being done, and we expect that we will complete that process within the next several weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If no such progress would have been made, the Chamber would have instructed you, Mr. Groome, to -- to include a report on the status of those concerns in an annex to the 2nd of April recertification notice. I'm a bit hesitant to do that at this moment, but I first address Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, do you think that the prospective of resolving the last 25 per cent are such that the Chamber could refrain from instructing Mr. Groome to include a specific report on those concerns in its 2nd of April filing, or do you say, No, the real problem will arise in the last 25 per cent; therefore, we'd like the Chamber to follow what it was inclined to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot say that the Prosecution is not working diligently trying to solve the problems, but -- and I cannot confirm the percentages because we just got some materials from the Prosecution. And if you bear with me, I prepared our position on this issue, or if you want me, we can file it in writing in a couple of days, whatever you would like me to do. To raise it now or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be best if you have prepared it that I invite Mr. Groome to make it part of the 2nd of April filing. Apparently there's no agreement on whether it's 75 per cent resolved, yes or no. What I also could suggest, most likely we'll not be able to finish in this first session, to see whether the parties could reach a joint approach on whether to use another two or three weeks to -- in -- in the confidence that the matter will be resolved or whether the parties would say, Let's make separate filings on it in the days to come. And of course if you would not agree on the approach, then of course the Chamber would instruct the parties whether or not to file something or whether to orally submit matters. Is there -- is this a suggestion which --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a very short observation. To date the Prosecution has disclosed approximately 144.000 individual documents. With the translations of those documents, it's about 250.000 documents altogether, and Mr. Lukic has identified some missing documents. So rather than to take this as an indication that the system is not working, I think this is a very strong indicator that the system is working. Mr. Lukic and his team are verifying what we say we disclosed, where there have been omissions. He's now bringing them to our attention very soon, and we are, in most cases, resolving them in the very week that the -- it is brought to our attention. For technical reasons 25 per cent of these particular set of documents will take some additional time. So I just want to make clear that it's the Prosecution's view that disclosure is always labour-intensive and sometimes difficult process, but I think that it is working well and the Prosecution certainly appreciates the diligence with which Mr. Lukic is verifying that we have provided everything that we say we have provided and giving us an opportunity to -- to fill the gaps where they exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps having listened to Mr. Groome who says, Well, the system is working pretty well but perhaps not for the last half a per cent, and as soon as we hear from Mr. Lukic that something is missing we immediately try to resolve that matter, I do not expect much from an annex to be attached to the 2nd of April filing, but perhaps it would be wiser to first listen to you and to hear what in your view the problems are before we take any further steps. So I invite you to make any oral submissions on the matter at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you give us an indication as to how much time you'd need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Five, six minutes probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five, six minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks. A new Rule 66(A)(ii) spreadsheet was provided by the Prosecution on or about 14th of February, 2012. This spreadsheet corrected the error of the previous spreadsheets which lacked ERN for many of the materials so disclosed. However, since that time we have raised with the Prosecution additional problems; namely, that we still cannot locate all the statements of the witnesses, particularly in B/C/S, even when reaching -- searching by ERN through the various methods that have been shown to us and advised to be used. Further, we have the problem that transcripts were not fully disclosed to us. This is a problem particularly for the proceedings before the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As in those cases the transcripts are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please read more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You -- please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in the cases dealt with before the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, transcripts are not publicly -- publicly available or readily obtainable, and unless someone has prepared transcripts for specific purposes, the standard practice is for only an audio recording in lieu of written transcript to be provided. Likewise, insofar as we have not been provided access to private closed-session materials from the ICTY cases we cannot readily locate the transcript said to be disclosed to us by the OTP. They have not disclosed to us any specific transcripts. I'm talking before reviewing those materials we received today. This is written before this Status Conference, and I didn't have time, and I didn't have the possibility to review the materials we received today. And the problem with this is two-folded. First, private and closed session -- sessions are not included, and second, the amount of B/C/S transcripts is very limited. So B/C/S translation of the transcripts. Under Rule 66(A)(ii), the obligation is up on the Prosecution to disclose statements in the language of the accused. In this case our client does not speak English, and he needs B/C/S transcripts. We cannot at this time confirm if audio materials or video materials have been provided by the OTP, because they have not identified for many of the transcripts any ERN by which we may locate the same among the voluminous disclosure that have been given to us by the Prosecution. As such, we consider at this point that the Prosecution has not fully complied with Rule 66(A)(ii). Your Honour already raised that the Prosecution didn't file the additional report on 12th of March, so that's -- we have to wait for that one as well. The purpose of Rule 66(A)(ii) is to enable the Defence to confront witnesses with all their prior statements and transcripts. The provision is of fundamental importance to the accused's right to a fair trial. It is an essential element of Rule 66(A)(ii) that the disclosure occur within a specific time limit so as to provide adequate time and resources for the accused to examine the material and prepare its case. In the instant case, we still do not have the materials and would ask as follows: The commence -- (a), the commencement of trial be postponed and not scheduled until the Prosecution has completed its obligation under Rule 66(A)(ii) in their entirety. And (b) order that no witness by the OTP may be called less than 90 days prior to the Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure having been completed in full, and we believe this is in line with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, especially the Karadzic case, where it said that cumulative effect of multiple disclosure violations resulted in an order that the Prosecution not be allowed to call any witness affected by late disclosure for a period of approximately 90 days to give Defence time to prepare. It is decision on accused 18th to 21st disclosure violation motions from 2nd November 2010 at paragraph 43. Mr. Mladic is not asking for any special treatment, just to what he's entitled to under the Rules and to be treated fairly and have the same rights and abilities to prepare for trial as other accused have had before him. Your Honour, this is what we had on this issue. Thank you for listening to us. And I say this is all under the reserve that we have to check the materials we received today from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. May I take it that you'll review that material as soon as possible so as to know whether it in any way effects the position taken by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we say that -- and perhaps it would also be wise to inform the Prosecution about that, because they'll file on the 2nd of April a motion, make submissions. Perhaps it would be where we suggested that perhaps any report on this matter should be attached to that one. I think it would be good for them to know as soon as possible whether what you receive today changes and to what extent changes your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you heard from my -- my learned friend Mr. Groome, it is pretty voluminous material, and we have this pre-trial brief due on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks to your extension of our time limit. So I'll try to involve as many team members as possible, but we are basically working on the pre-trial brief right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I cannot promise that it will be done before the end of the next week, but then it would be too late for a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unless Mr. Groome would spend a separate submission on specifically addressing what -- what you said today and also including any change in your position possibly by the end of next week. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Four quick points, Your Honour, just in response to Mr. Lukic. Lest there be any confusion about whether or not the Prosecution has diligently complied with its responsibilities under Rule 66(A)(ii), I inform the Chamber that on the 3rd of October, 2011, four months before the Prosecution filed its witness list, it provided most of the prior statements of the people it intended to place or provisionally believed it would place on its witness list. I think this is unprecedented in that the Defence has been provided Rule 66(A)(ii) material prior to the identification of a witness in a witness list. Two, with respect to the materials from the courts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would point out that the Prosecution has disclosed all 66(A)(ii) material that we are in possession of. The Prosecution does not understand its obligation under Rule 66(A)(ii) to require it to go to the courts of Bosnia and to inquire whether witnesses have testified there and to secure that testimony. The Prosecution's obligation is limited, as we understand our responsibility, to materials in our possession. Thirdly, Your Honour, with respect to the provision of audiotapes, Mr. Lukic is expressing a preference for B/C/S transcripts of prior testimony. Again what is in the Prosecution's reasonable possession are audiotapes of a witness's prior testimony here before the Tribunal. The B/C/S transcriptions are not routinely made. The Prosecution believes that it fulfils its obligation under Rule 66(A)(ii) by providing audiotapes of those prior testimonies. We do not understand our obligation under Rule 66(A)(ii) to require us to secure B/C/S transcribers to go through the testimonies from previous trials and transcribe for the purposes of disclosure. And finally Mr. Lukic has expressed some frustration or difficulty with respect to finding transcripts in that they do not have ERN numbers. I believe Mr. Lukic will recall that Ms. Stewart earlier this week explained the special file names that are assigned to transcripts. They are not given evidence numbers. They are given a different name or under a different coding system which essentially is the case number, the date, and the page number of the transcript, and I believe that problem has already been corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may summarise. I do not think that Mr. Lukic expressed concerns about the diligence with which the Prosecution made efforts to meet its obligations under Rule 66(A)(ii), and even might appreciate that the Prosecution started very early. I think what he said is that since it's not complete, that causes us problems. There are two other matters, whether Rule 66(A)(ii) would extend to anything which is not in the possession of the Prosecution or not yet in the possession of the Prosecution, and the question whether disclosure of audio material would meet the obligations under Rule 66(A)(ii) are legal matters which we'll look at. The last issued raised, the fourth one, was of a rather practical nature and referred to efforts by Ms. Stewart to assist in resolving the problem. The Prosecution is now, I take it, well aware of the position taken by the Defence. The first thing that should happen is that, Mr. Lukic, that you, as soon as possible, inform the Prosecution whether what you received today changes in any way your position, and then we'll wait for the further submissions. And we are aware that if Mr. Groome, if the Prosecution, would include, which it is instructed to do if it goes beyond what was said today, if the Prosecution then would include further submissions on this matter in its 2nd of April filing, and if you, Mr. Lukic, would then present any further submissions not later than by the end of next week. Is that -- I see you're agreeing with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber will then further consider that matter. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm reminded, Mr. Lukic, that your initial complaints were put in an e-mail but were never formally filed, and now since it looks as if we get real litigation on the matter, you are hereby also instructed to file, apart from what you would like to add in the present situation, also to file the initial e-mail you had sent so that we have a full record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other matter in relation to this? If not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I was just informed if it's possible to have a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic needs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take the usual break now. I don't think that we'll need more than 45 minutes to one hour after the break. We'll take a break and we will resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I resume. Mr. Lukic, I instructed you to formally file the e-mail which introduced this whole issue. Could you do that by the end of this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I move on. On the 28th of February, 2012, the Prosecution has filed a motion requesting that the Chamber vacate the 12th of March, 2012, deadline for its Rule 68(i) disclosure and proposed an alternative disclosure procedure. On the 5th of March, the Defence filed a response opposing the motion and the proposed alternative disclosure procedure. It further submitted that should the motion be granted, the commencement of the trial date should be delayed. On the 6th of March the Chamber informed the parties through an informal communication that it denied the Prosecution's alternative disclosure procedure but granted a fixed time extension of three weeks from 12th of March, 2012, until the 2nd of April. The Chamber denied without prejudice the Defence's request for delaying the start of the trial. And this decision is here placed on the record. Now, in relation to this decision, the Chamber calls the parties's attention to its approach of requiring that disclosure be completed by a specific date as opposed to rolling deadlines throughout the course of the trial. On the 23rd of March, the Prosecution filed a request for reconsideration of the Chamber's decision, and in light of the fact that the current deadline is the 2nd of April, the Chamber considered it appropriate to shorten the defence response time so as to be able to hear from the Defence before the deadline expires. At the 65 ter meeting, the Defence explained that it would be unable to respond before the 4th of April, which is of course after the current deadline of the 2nd of April. Therefore, the Chamber puts on the record that the Defence response is due by the 4th of April and hereby grants an extension of the Prosecution's 2 April Rule 68(i) disclosure deadline until such time as the Chamber issues its final decision on the request for reconsideration. The Chamber informs the parties that it aims to have a final decision issued as soon as possible after the response is filed. At the 23rd February Status Conference, the Chamber announced that the Electronic Disclosure System, known as EDS, that submissions in relation to that system were now closed and that it would issue a decision on the matter in a week. The Prosecution requested that any decision be postponed to allow for further negotiations between the parties. The Chamber instructed the parties to report to the Chamber if a decision was still needed, and if so, on which outstanding matters. On the 2nd of March, 2012, the Defence filed a report indicating that there were certain ongoing unresolved issues and maintaining its earlier requests for relief. On the 16th of March, the Prosecution filed its response to the Defence report, reiterating its position that the Defence's requests for relief should be denied. Now, these filings were all discussed at the Rule 65 ter meeting, and I will briefly summarise what seemed to be the unresolved issues. First, the issue of identifying meta-data in the EDS and the parallel hard disk disclosure. The Prosecution takes the position that there is obligation to provide this under the Rules. The Defence does not assert that this is necessarily required by the Rules but stresses the degree to which its work is frustrated without this meta-data information. In relation to this, the Prosecution offered to arrange a training session for the Defence staff at the Belgrade field office on search techniques and other alternatives to using meta-data to locate documents. The Prosecution is to provide an update on this training meeting today. Mr. Groome, could you inform us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I can just correct one thing the Chamber said. Although the Prosecution rejects any notion that it is required to provide such data under the Rules, it has endeavoured to do so and continues to endeavour to do that because it does appreciate that it does facilitate the preparations of the Defence. With respect to training, earlier today I met with Mr. Lukic, and he is still considering whether this is necessary. We are ready to respond quickly at any time to assist Mr. Lukic in making sure that his staff has any training that we can provide or any technical advice we can provide how to most efficiently navigate and search the materials disclosed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Any further comment, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just briefly stress that our team does not need training, because I have several team members who have been using EDS for six, seven, or even ten years. What we were complaining about is the lack of this meta-data, because even if we find 300 documents at once listed without meta-data, we cannot use that. So the training is not necessary. What we need is possibility to meaningfully search the documents put into EDS. And I was offered by Mr. Groome to use their -- to see if we can use their office in Belgrade only in terms of speeding up the search because they have different transmitting system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll come to that in a second. I would like to refer now to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Training -- training we don't need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say this in a very firm way. I do understand that you have troubles in achieving what you want to achieve without the meta-data, and I do understand that the offer for training is that by using alternatives to this, that you might achieve, if not all, then at least part of what you're seeking anyhow. Now, I do not know to what extent you have discussed the content of that training. If I'm offered training on a certain matter, I'd first like to know exactly what the training was about before I can conclude that I do not need it. I don't know to what extent this has been explored and to what extent, if only partially, it would help out whether meta-data are not complete yet. But before saying that I can't learn anything more, I'm usually hesitant to do that. This is just an observation. I don't know in what detail the content of the training was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll take your advance -- advice and see if we can learn anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I would like to add is that while creating EDS system, I was consulted how to advance it, because I was using ZyLAB even before that, and I was trying to solve the problem of the technicians of ICTY had how to search numbers or how to search Cyrillic, and I have then at that time -- maybe they developed something I'm not aware at this moment, but what I'm telling you is really what we need is just meta-data and then we will be perfectly capable of searching all the documents in the EDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was not suggesting, Mr. Lukic, that you are not an expert or close to an expert in the system. The only thing I was saying is that before refusing an offer for further training, I would always explore exactly what it could bring me or not, and I again have no opinion about this, whether you have explored that. I just made that observation. And it may well be that it's superfluous and that you did everything you would possibly be expected to do before saying, We don't need it. I leave that alone. The only thing I'm trying as always to seek to what extent the Chamber, sometimes by just putting questions, can assist the parties in resolving problems. I think that the meta-data, of course, a lot of work is done on that already, and I did not understand the Prosecution to offer the training replacing further work on the meta-data, but, rather, to assist the Defence in perhaps being able to move on if not perhaps in the most perfect way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- yes. I'll now come to the second issue, which was the slow speed of the -- yes, Mr. Groome. I see you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm just standing up to report. I didn't mean to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To report on the offered --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You had asked us to investigate a suggestion I had made at the 65 ter meeting and report today, so I was just -- I thought you were going to invite me to make a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- no, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've agreed in meetings with Mr. Lukic today that we will conduct a test regarding the speed of the EDS when remotely accessed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I wanted to introduce the speed issue separately, so I interrupted Mr. Lukic, and I'm going to interrupt you as well but give you an opportunity, because the second issue which was discussed was the slow speed of the EDS via remote access. The parties agree that this is not within the Prosecution's control and also that the EDS speed is significantly slower via remote access as opposed to within the Defence rooms in the Tribunal. And in relation to this, Mr. Groome, you had proposed that perhaps the Defence could explore whether it's possible to have access to a computer in the Belgrade field office and, if so, co-ordinate this through the Registry. Mr. Lukic, you were invited or you are invited to explore this issue with the Registry, and I'd like to receive any updates on these matters. And that apparently you were about to give, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just so the Chamber fully understands the issue, the Belgrade field office of the ICTY relies on a direct satellite link and not on the local internet provider. So Mr. Lukic and myself have agreed to the following: The Registry does not have extra computers which -- which Mr. Lukic can test the -- the speed of the -- the satellite link. The Office of the Prosecutor does have some spare computers down there, and I have arranged for Mr. Lukic to conduct a testing of both systems by running the same search from the internet terminal in his office and running that very same search on the internet terminal in the field office. If Mr. Lukic finds that there is a significant increase in speed such that it would assist him in using the EDS system through the Belgrade field office, I have agreed to explore with the Prosecutor and the Registrar the possibility of making a permanent computer and work space available to the Mladic Defence team, one that would respect the confidentiality of Defence preparations and would likewise be isolated from OTP and Registry files. So if Mr. Lukic after conducting such a test believes there's such a benefit, all he need do is inform me and then I will explore the matter further, and we can arrange for this test in a day or two. So I would simply ask Mr. Lukic to advise us when he would like to conduct this test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any further comments on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I move to the third issue which was discussed in this context, which is the summary information contained in the EDS short description of the Mladic case-specific EDS indexes. During the discussions at the Rule 65 ter meeting, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to file a report at the end of April as to the resolution of this issue, and the Chamber hereby puts that instruction on the record and further instructs the Prosecution that the report should address: (1) whether the collections and related indexes are complete, (2) whether the summary information has been sufficiently augmented upon completion of the collections and indexes, and (3) if not complete when it is expected to be completed. That was the third issue. I don't think that there will be any need for comments, but ... Then I move to the final issue. The final issue being Mr. Mladic's access to the Electronic Disclosure System in the United Nations Detention Unit. According to an informal update received from OLAD on the 23rd of March, this issue is now resolved, and Mr. Mladic now has secure access from a computer in the UNDU. And, Mr. Lukic, you're unable to confirm this at Monday's 65 ter meeting. Can you now confirm that that matter has been properly arranged?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Technically, yes; but in practice, no. Since Mr. Mladic hasn't received any training yet, and he was just telling me an hour ago that the technician who was -- who is in charge actually of training him would be away until the 11th of the next month. So before that date he wouldn't be able to start receiving any kind of training.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he would be able to use that computer and share with others and would be able only to use it maybe couple of hours a day depending on the schedule. So it is something that is still in practice pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think it was considered to provide additional training to Mr. Mladic anyhow. I think we then should further explore when that training could take place, by whom it would be given, and, of course, then we would further have to explore the availability of the computer. I can imagine that it requires some arranging between various detainees. But the technical part, then, has been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't expect the Prosecution to be able to say much about training of Mr. Mladic on -- in computer skills, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be very inappropriate for us to have anything to do with that, so I would like to state on the record that we couldn't have anything to do with that kind of training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, I was not even thinking of you providing that training but even to be able to say anything about the problem in itself, perhaps apart from that if Mr. Mladic would need training, that you would applaud if he would receive it, but that's a kind of very sweeping general statement which doesn't assist greatly. Then I take it that this will be further explored with OLAD. Have you taken initiatives already in that direction, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just learned from Mr. Mladic that there are some impediments regarding this training. I would try to see with the UNDU management if they can allow me to spend maybe an hour or two tomorrow with Mr. Mladic showing him basics and probably somebody else would be able to show him much more. Of course, he will be needing a translator at the same time, because everybody else who is using this system in the UNDU speak English, so for Mr. Mladic who doesn't speak English would also be very difficult to use the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say apart from training, language issues may arise as well. One second, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the practicalities of what has now been technically prepared need further attention and not to forget about the language issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic, the Defence report maintains the relief requested in its prior submissions on these issues. Now, in light of the Rule 65 ter meeting discussions and the fact that Defence made three submissions in addition to its 2nd of March report, the Chamber requests that you specify exactly what relief you are requesting and whether you seek a decision by the Chamber or wish to continue negotiations with the Prosecution. And I'd like to give you an opportunity to explain that now. So not further to argue why you need it or why it's reasonable, but what subject matters -- on which subject matters you seek relief in a decision by the Chamber and on what matters you think that continuing negotiations with the Prosecution or with OLAD would at this moment the most appropriate way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would maintain all our requests emphasised in those four motions, especially in the motion from -- filed on 9th of February, 2012. Basically it comes to -- again we have to come back to meta-data, to have all meta-data disclosed. And we discovered that having the documents only in the EDS and through ZyLAB would allow only the team members that work with ZyLAB to be able to search the documents. For example, we wouldn't be able to give any document to an expert witness in the format we have. So, again, the Defence, although the Prosecution has completely different view -- but the Defence would prefer to have the documents in tiff or pdf format to be able --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- to give it to the witnesses and the potential witnesses and to expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, your request to have it either in tiff or pdf, help me because my recollection might not be complete in that. Had you asked for that in the motions, the submissions you made until now, or is it a new matter you're raising?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We did -- give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, my staff confirms that you did. So it was just -- I hope you understand that my recollection does not always serves me well enough and then I just ask assistance to refresh my memory, but that apparently is not new. Yes, any other relief you would like to -- meta-data, pdf and tiff format for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
