utterances.text: Either or. Or if they have half in pdf, half in tiff, we would accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you do not need them in both formats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, anything else remaining?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's it on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's this on this topic, because I do understood you also asked for Mr. Mladic to have access to the EDS from the UNDU, and that, of course, has been technically resolved so that relief is not requested any further, although there is a remaining training problem and availability problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And if we have pdf or tiff format, we would be able to provide the documents to Mr. Mladic, then he would be able to use and search all the documents on his convenient time. Unlike -- and not only during the time period he would be allocated that one computer they have in UNDU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say he would then not need access to EDS for doing that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's what you wanted to bring to our attention as far as remaining relief is concerned. If you would give me one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to clarify matters, Mr. Lukic. In the 9th of February filing, you requested re-disclosure of all the material. Is that still a relief you are seeking?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we need all the materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On -- on the basis you -- you set out. Then second, postponement of the start of the trial until all the meta-data issues have been resolved, that also stands?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any comments in relation to what I just discussed with Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Only that Ms. Stewart informs me that presently there are -- many of the documents are in tiff form. Many are in pdf form. There are some documents in Word form and I believe that's as a Word document, and I believe that's the material that causes Mr. Lukic to make this application to have re-disclosure. And just to remind the Chamber that the present regime of second disclosure was done in full consultation with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No further comments, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, I think that batches eight -- seven and eight have those multi -- multipage tiff or multipage pdf format documents disclosed to us. Otherwise, anything prior to that was only in the single-page tiff format which cannot be used as a document. Only you can utilise it through utilising ZyLAB or EDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any technical comments on that? I must say single-page tiff documents ring a bell to me. Getting one page and then unable to look at the rest, that is something that is very familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We would need to time to verify that, but at present I have no basis for contradicting what Mr. Lukic said. Ms. Stewart does inform me that beginning of that batch, a different format was used to facilitate uploading the documents into ZyLAB at Mr. Lukic's request, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If there are no further comments on this, then I'd like to move to the final issue in relation to disclosure is the material within the tracking unit files. Mr. Groome, at the Rule 65 ter meeting you stayed that disclosure of this material was scheduled to be concluded this week, and my question is, although the week is not over yet, whether disclosure is now complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, today the Prosecution has disclosed all of the documents in this category of documents. I would ask Mr. Lukic to review what has been disclosed today as soon as possible and we'll address any problems he perceives as quickly as possible, but it is our belief we have fully disclosed everything in this category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. Mr. Lukic, if there are any remaining issues, then you'll know how to approach Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move on to the adjudicated facts. On the 28th of February this year, the Trial Chamber issued its first decision on adjudicated facts. In this decision, it instructed the Prosecution to file an amendment to its witness list within two weeks of the filing of the decision in relation to time estimates for witnesses whose evidence is to be adjusted and to indicate which witnesses will be withdrawn. On the 13th of March, the Prosecution filed it's submissions on amending its witness list in light of the Chamber's first decision on adjudicated facts in which it stated that the Prosecution is not in a position to amend its witness list and that it will defer any decision in this regard until the Chamber issues a decision on the rebuttal evidence procedure. The Chamber accepts the approach outlined in the Prosecution's filing to defer amending its witness list until a decision on the rebuttal evidence procedure is filed. However, the Prosecution should expect a shortened deadline of no more than a week after the filing of the Chamber's decision. I further stress that the Prosecution should already be preparing now instead of beginning to work on this after the filing of the decision. Any questions or comments in relation to the adjudicated facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has already begun its analysis, but I don't want the Chamber to underestimate the amount of work that that involves. For each adjudicated fact may be the product of the evidence of several witnesses, maybe dozens of documents. It's really a very time-consuming and detailed process of -- of sorting out what evidence can be safely withdrawn in reliance on it, and of course if we get that wrong, we could find ourselves at the end of the trial having failed to meet our trial burden. So it's a task that we take very seriously. We've already begun the process and one we will do as diligently and carefully as we can. And of course we will always strive to meet deadlines imposed by the Chamber, but I do want the Chamber to fully appreciate the amount of work that's involved and this is all in addition to the many other tasks that we are engaged in in preparing for trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should have phrased it differently. Perhaps I should have said I'd further like to stress that the Chamber is fully confident that the Prosecution had already begun by preparing now and that the Chamber would not have thought of the Prosecution beginning to work on this only after the filing of the decision. That might have been a more positive way of sending exactly the same message. There was no misunderstanding about what kind of work it takes to deal with those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move on to the agreed facts. On the 16th of March, the parties have filed their fifth joint submission on the progress of negotiations on agreed facts which contained all those facts to which the parties have agreed and also an update on negotiations regarding potential agreement about certain facts relating to the Defence's alibi notices. This report was discussed at Monday's -- this Monday's Rule 65 ter meeting, and at that same meeting the parties also discussed possible agreement in relation to the Philipps expert report. In relation to the possibility of agreement upon facts relating to the Defence's alibi notices, the parties were instructed to resume negotiations. I now inform the parties that these negotiations should be addressed in the parties' joint agreed facts submissions which are due for the 27th of April of this year. Mr. Groome, also in relation to this same issue, the Prosecution's Rule 67(B)(ii) alibi rebuttal notice which was filed on the 16th of March includes 14 new witnesses and 32 documents that the Prosecution seeks to add to its Rule 65 ter (E)(ii) lists. At page 2 of the notice it states that each witness will cover one of five categories. The Chamber is particularly interested in three of these categories, specifically Mladic's travel to or from Belgrade, Mladic's presence/whereabouts in Belgrade, and Mladic's presence in Belgrade during the noticed period. Mr. Groome, the Chamber wonders to what extent these new witnesses and the additional evidence of witnesses already on your witness list relate to matters that the Prosecution would otherwise be willing to agree to. Therefore the Prosecution is instructed to inform the Trial Chamber by the 27th of April whether it maintains its rebuttal alibi notice request for additional of these witnesses and documents to its witness and evidence lists or whether some may, in fact, no longer be needed in light of the agreed facts negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour, but if I could express some of the difficulties that maybe the Chamber did not fully appreciate when it gave us that deadline. The alibi essentially is that Mr. Mladic attended some meetings and was present at a wedding, and the Chamber gave us 29 days to investigate that. The alibi centres around this wedding that took place some 17 years ago. The Prosecution understands as one of its most important functions to make sure that the Chamber has before it credible and reliable evidence to be able to accurately adjudicate issues related to this. We have done our best. We have tried to identify the witnesses that we believe are necessary for this, but I must say I'm not confident that we have identified all of the relevant evidence as yet. For example, I can informed the Chamber that we have come across a video of Mr. Mladic in the VMA hospital dated the 16th of July in which he appears in his uniform as opposed to his suit, but his wife appears to be in the same dress she appears in the wedding pictures and seems to have the same floral corsage on her dress that she is wearing at the wedding. I don't know whether this has been an inadvertent -- Mr. Mladic has simply forgotten about this, but the Prosecution, again, in trying to make sure that we do have all of the evidence necessary so that the Chamber can make accurate finds with respect to this is still continuing to investigate helicopter logs, travel logs, and doing our best to investigate all of this. Certainly we will not call any evidence about a matter with which we -- there's agreement or with which there's a judiciously noticed fact, but I must impress upon the Chamber that it -- I'm not sure that before the 27th of April we will have been able to fully investigate this event 17 years ago. Of course with all the other things we are doing, we are doing our best to do so and we will keep the Chamber informed about our progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see how far you can come and of course this deadline is set, and if you would seek an extension showing good cause to say we have been able to explore this and this and this but not yet that and that and that or we are still waiting for -- to find three or five witnesses, then of course we would consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to the Philipps expert report, Mr. McCloskey, you were to meet with the Defence's staff to see if there was any potential agreement on the charts and lists contained in the expert report. Has such a meeting taken place, and could you give any information about progress that may have been made?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As it transpired, it was myself and Mr. Lukic who spoke about it. And I think it's probably more appropriate for Mr. Lukic to restate his position rather than having me do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we are now at a third person involved. Mr. Lukic, we await your comments on observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Regarding Mr. Philipps, the Defence stands by its position that Philipps is not qualified to be an expert under Rule 94 bis. The reports authored by Philipps are not appropriate under Rule as expert reports, that the same are erroneous, unreliable and not credible. We believe that jurisprudence of the Rule 94 bis and expert reports have certain standards that have to be followed, and we would direct your attention to the case law of Blagojevic and Jokic where it's -- and, for example, on their judgement from 17 January 2005 at paragraph 27, and also there is jurisprudence on Milutinovic where portions of expert testimony excluded but beyond the direct knowledge and expertise of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Lukic, you're now addressing a matter which I invited you to ignore for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You remember what we said during the 65 ter meeting; that is, irrespective of whether you expect -- or whether you accept Mr. Philipps as an expert, is what we find in the tables could nevertheless be true or not true. And of course I asked you to focus on that primarily, because if you would agree on the accuracy of the tables irrespective of whether they were made by Mr. Philipps or a housewife or whomever, if the outcome is correct, if you could agree on that, then of course you could even leave any further discussion about the qualities of Mr. Philipps apart. That's what I asked you to focus on. Would you preferably first address that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Philipps was proposed to be an expert witness, so we cannot go beyond that. We have to address that issue first. And we don't want to take the path that can lead us to the practice that persons not qualified as experts could be -- or their work could be accepted as expert work. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It misses the point I made, Mr. Lukic. If someone who is not knowledgeable by chance produces a chart which would reflect the composition of certain army units, and if you say you have -- you're not qualified to do that, but by chance the result is accurate, then it's not accepting the work of the expert any more, but then it comes down to agreeing on the accuracy of a chart and then you strike out that it was made by Mr. Philipps or by your next door neighbour or by the grocery shop at the corner, and then you agree on what facts are contained in there, and that's what I asked you to focus on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, we cannot confirm anything done by Mr. Philipps, and we do not have the obligation to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about obligations. I invited you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to look at the accuracy of a chart and to forget about who produced it. If it's accurate in your view, and if it's accurate in the view of the Prosecution, you could agree on the accuracy of a chart. That is what we asked you to do, and from what I hear now is more or less that you say, I don't want to look at it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bear with me for a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow us, we would use help of Mr. Petrusic, who is more an expert on that issue like Mr. McCloskey, and he would check the charts, but we cannot do it before the next -- next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you'll still be there after next Wednesday, isn't it? Then I suggest that Mr. Petrusic and Mr. McCloskey sit together, look at the chart, forget about who produced them, and see whether it accurately reflects what it says it reflects.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then to see to what extent you could agree. Perhaps you agree on 90 per cent but not on the last 5 per cent or not at all. I'm not suggesting anything. But that is specifically what I asked you to do in your conversations with the Prosecution. And I understand that on from the middle of next week you'll give it a try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then may I take it that we'll then receive any -- an update on -- on whatever results from these conversations in the agreed facts progress report, which is -- is due for the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrusic I take it has now better understood what we discussed during the last 65 ter meeting where, of course, he was not present. Then I'd like to move on unless there are any further comments on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honour, can I consult -- consult with my client for one or two minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If it assists you, I've got two more pages to go, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I move on to the expert reports. On the 20th of February, the Defence has filed its Rule 94 bis (B) notice and objection in relation to the witness Philipps and his proposed expert report. You also may notice, Mr. Lukic, that earlier I dealt with agreed facts, and now I'm dealing with expert reports. That's not the same category exactly, and I think the discussions are to take place perhaps based on charts which by chance resulted from someone working on something which you considered not expert work, but I now move to the reports. The Defence filed its Rule 94 bis notice and objection in relation to Witness Philipps and his proposed expert report. On the 23rd of February, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to file the proposed expert report, and that is what the Prosecution did on the 24th of February. On the 6th of March, 2012, the Defence filed a supplemental notice to the original Rule 94 bis notice and objection in relation to Witness Philipps in which the Defence stated that it may file additional notices. On the 7th of March the Chamber informed the parties that the Defence has until the 26th of March to file any additional notices, following which the Prosecution has two weeks to respond. Also on the 7th of March, the Prosecution requested the Chamber's permission to file a single response to all the Defence's Rule 94 bis notices regarding Witness Philipps, and on the 9th of March, through an informal communication, the Chamber informed the Prosecution that it could file a single response to the multiple defence notices. That decision is hereby put on the record. At the Rule 65 ter meeting, the Prosecution was instructed to file a corrigendum to its pre-trial report by the end of this week. The corrigendum is to update the category "status of reports," that column in Annex C of the report, and make directions in relation to Witness Dean Manning and that instruction is hereby also put on the record. Finally, also at the Rule 65 ter meeting, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence that the expert report of witness General Dannatt is expected to be finalised on the 23rd of April and filed shortly thereafter. Mr. Lukic, perhaps unnecessarily, but I remind you that the Defence 30-day notice deadline begin running from the date of filing of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any comments or questions in relation to expert reports? If not, I move to the next item on my agenda, which is an invitation to the parties and to the accused, Mr. Mladic, to address the Chamber on any additional matter. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This relates to disclosure. On the 19th of September, 2011, the Prosecution on its own initiative filed a first Prosecution report on pre-trial preparations. The Chamber will recall that in paragraph 2 of that submission the Prosecution considered that filing such reports would assist the Pre-Trial Judge in discharging your responsibilities under the Rules, and particularly Rule 65 ter (B), an oversight of the disclosure of materials under Rule 66 and 68. The Chamber will also recall that in paragraphs 7 to 32, the Prosecution set out in a very detailed and transparent way the procedures that we would follow to discharge this most important duty. In any -- in addition to the objections raised by Mr. Lukic, the Prosecution recognises it has an independent obligation to disclose potentially exculpatory material. As the Appeals Chamber in the Karemera and Bralo cases has reminded us, it is one of our most important functions and it is an independent obligation. We are bound to discharge this duty irrespective of whether Mr. Mladic -- the Mladic Defence demands materials or complains about the way in which we conduct our reviews. We have also done this in a detailed and transparent way so that the Chamber may, irrespective of any complain, that the Defence advise the Prosecution whether it is of the view that we are complying with the -- in our disclosure practices with the Rules and the relevant jurisprudence. To date the Trial Chamber has not directed the Prosecution to amend its review procedures. We understand this to be an affirmation that we are discharging our responsibilities in a way consistent with the Rules and jurisprudence -- and jurisprudence. If we have misinterpreted this, it would be helpful for the Chamber to make its views known before we complete this review process which now is in its final weeks. Obviously should the Chamber find any significant fault in the way we have conducted our reviews, we will have to change our review procedures, and we will have to adapt our work accordingly. Knowing this prior to discharging the legal consultants and reviewers specifically hired for this project would be most appreciated by the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. It will not come as a surprise to you that I will not immediately respond to this, and I think you were quite optimistic that you thought that I would recall paragraphs 7 to 32 of a certain submission. I think I have a relatively well overview, but I would really first have to re-read that, then discuss it with my colleagues and with the Chambers staff, and then we'll consider what response will be given to the observations you just made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If any. I repeat that because you had said you would appreciate to have it affirmed by the Chamber. Of course, we will first have to consider whether we can affirm it, yes or no, and whether it would be for us to affirm it or -- but again I have to re-read a lot of materials. I have to re-read your submissions and then to think about it, and then you'll finally know whether and in what way the Chamber responds to what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We appreciate the Chamber's consideration of the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other matter, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any matter to be raised in addition to what we have discussed today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The members of the Defence team have nothing else to add. Maybe Mr. Mladic would like to address the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He was the next one. I said that -- that I would invite the parties and the accused, of course. Mr. Mladic, is there anything you'd like to add or to raise which is appropriately be raised at a Status Conference? If there's anything, please proceed. If you prefer to remain seated, I would not object to that. I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not like to be ironic. You did put it rightly here that I am seated in the courtroom. The security can sit down, and I would like the camera to zoom in on me. I will not be making any gestures. I merely want them to see that I'm alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, there are standing instructions for what is on what camera. There are six cameras here. One of them certainly is upon you. I think everyone who has followed these proceedings knows that you are alive. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, I did tell you earlier that time is endless, and I did make a graph that I gave to Mr. Petrusic. He hails from the mount of Romanija where I spent the better part of my life during the war defending, as far as I was able to, the mount of Romanija as well as the other mountains, the Knin area and beyond, all the way to the VMA; and as the gentleman said, how come I was wearing a uniform in the VMA? And since I am in the courtroom, I will sit down so that the security need not be on their feet, and can you please tell me how many minutes do I have at my disposal to speak because I do have some observations to make, some of which you may like and others perhaps not, and then I will sit down and speak in detail, because I'm interested in the truth and nothing but the truth. I am not defending myself, and I am the one who knows my own mind the best, and I want all those who gave some -- whatever sort of statements, who liked me or disliked me to be called here either by telephone or by videolink or in writing in a language that I am familiar with. I would like all these to be given to me, because I received those two indictments from the Prosecution. I am a person of advanced age, nearly 70. I was born on the 8th of March, 1943. That was another thing that I wanted to correct. There was an error. You said that you were a good mathematician, and I immediately calculated 70 plus 22, that's 92, and then if you deduct, you get to 41. Perhaps I could be granted 41 minutes to speak, and if need be, you can interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, first of all, the security acts in accordance with their instructions. That's what they're going to do and they're happy to stand if that's in their instructions. That's point one. Second, you may have noticed that matters like receiving all the material was, although perhaps in a very technical way, part of our discussions today and of last Monday. Now, the time you would need depends very much on whether you can be focused on matters which are appropriately raised during a Status Conference. Therefore, I would suggest try to be focused. Clearly indicate what matter you want to address and then do it as efficiently as possible. We will follow what you say and then I would say if you could finish in -- well, let's say in 15 minutes, that would be appreciated. If that's not possible, I would grant you 20 minutes, as long as you keep focused on what is appropriately raised in a Status Conference. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do agree 20 minutes, and, lads, you can sit down. Thank you very much, Mr. Orie. I made a note of what I'm about to say to you. Firstly, time is running away for both you and I. I am in no hurry. The only question remains of who is going to be the first one to join the one up there. I will not be attacking those who are prosecuting me. Mr. Wilkomski [as interpreted], perhaps, a Pole; or Mr. Groome, is he of Germanic origin; and you, according to the information I have, you're a Dutchman, I have nothing against that. I appreciate the fact that you were born, that you are alive and that you represent this Tribunal that was set up by the UN Security Council. Whatever the circumstances involved, I will not be going into that. Both you and I are interested in the truth, and where it comes to the truth, I need to raise certain issues for reasons of my health. First of all, my right side of the body is numb. I still have not regained my full feeling for the right leg and hand, and that's why it's difficult for me to handle the mouse. It's true that I was given, as Mr. Lukic said, in room number 7 an hour or an hour and a half to work on the computer, but I'm still unable to access the system. Mr. Yaqub [phoen], who I think is some sort of an expert, will be away until the 11th of April. I settled the matter with Mr. Petrov, who is a native of Bulgaria and is a representative of this Tribunal, as well as with Mr. Kennedy. I wrote a request, and he told me that another expert would be assigned to me. I also asked for an interpreter because what am I to do with somebody who is knowledgeable about it if don't know English? I have a password that was given to me for that machine, and this is the password that only I and you and perhaps your superior Ban Ki-Moon can be aware of. Let me mention him as well whom has rewarded you as Judges and the Prosecutor as well, whereas those who are defending me are not really boasting with the pay they get. They are silent on the matter which means that things aren't that good. But let us proceed. You say a fair trial and I am all for it. You can prosecute me and convict me to your liking. Am I guilty? Am I innocent? And to what extent? That is all in your hands. What am I complaining of? Statistics. You, not you personally, but those who established the Tribunal, they also established the procedure; i.e., what the guard will look like, what the Judge will look like, what the Prosecution will wear, what my lawyers will wear, what the staff will look like. I suppose they come from the Registry. And this gentleman here as well. I can have no influence over that, and nor can my Defence. Your procedure is something that everybody's supposed to adhere to. I know that I am in prison. I know that I was given the permission to go to room number 7, but I am not -- I have not been trained to work on the computer. I have my password, but if I give it to my -- to the interpreter and to the policeman who was helping me get my way with the computer, then I -- they changed the password and they get me -- they give me a new password the following day. But I am very slow, and I've only been given an hour or 45 minutes in certain intervals, and because of my health condition, it takes me very long to read one page. For instance, this one page I took the whole day to write. So I need to have an opportunity of not an hour and 45 minutes, but more. Can I be allowed in that room number 7 to train myself at the expense of my sleep time? There are various colleagues there from Seselj to others, Croats, Muslims, Albanians who are there with me, but I need to have time enough to read these documents. You've given me the indictment on several occasions. Mr. Lukic, Mr. Saljic all brought the indictment to me, but it takes me time to read it. Everything that has been adjudicated, it may be the best in terms of your legal profession that I know nothing of. It may be the Holy Scripture, perhaps even more than that, but I will not accept anything that's been adjudicated, X, Y, Z, in any other part of the world. I am at trial here. Do not deny Lukic of anything. Do not interfere with him. Mr. Groome and Mr. McCloskey and their team, they can swamp us with whatever they want. Mr. Groome, if you want me, I can tell you about the wedding, and I can tell you what sort of underwear I was wearing at the VMA, and you can't possibly know that without me. And you have no right to exert pressure on my wife or my family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. I try to assist you in keeping focused. The issue of time available on the computer and additional training, we discussed earlier that that would be further explored, and that's what's going to happen. That's one. Second, adjudicated facts. You said you opposed to anything, to accept any adjudicated fact. Well, that's more or less what Mr. Lukic said in his response to the Prosecution's motion. So therefore, what you're telling us now has been -- I'd say has been clearly expressed by Mr. Lukic and doesn't need any further consideration apart from that to the extent the Chamber has decided on the motion which until now was in two decisions that apparently Mr. Lukic is seeking to appeal those decisions and the Prosecution will respond to that. We'll deal with those matters in an orderly legal procedural matter. And if you say but it's you that all defined what the rules are here, I can tell you that that is true for all the legal systems in the world, that it's the -- those responsible for the system, they adopt the rules, and those who are in that system in whatever position, Prosecution, Defence, accused, Judges, they will have to abide by those rules. Could you please then move on to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Judge, I would not like to appear incoherent. Let me just say that on the 16th of July, 1995, and the VMA and me wearing the uniform, can I just be allowed to say something about it? Can I clarify this issue so that it's easier for you, the Prosecution, and my soul? From what I remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I said you can address whatever you want what can be appropriately be addressed during a Status Conference. At a Status Conference, the content of evidence or potential evidence is not to be discussed. I even would stress that by explaining now how it all was, we find ourselves in the situation that we are discussing potential evidence, that you're giving a statement where you might even create prejudice for yourself. I would advise you to seek the advice of Mr. Lukic whether or not to further expound on those evidentiary matters. I can assure you that the issue of whereabouts in the context of an alibi will be fully explored and litigated as far as I can see it now, apart from those portions where, apparently, the parties seem to agree on your whereabouts. Mr. Lukic, I'll give you an opportunity to consult with your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Please proceed, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Orie. Once I start going, I have a tendency to raise my voice, but this is due to my medical condition, so please forgive me. I know that this could be irritating, so please feel free to criticise me for that. Now, as for the number of witnesses, there was some mention of that, and I am insisting that all potential witnesses, as well as those who had given statements, and I accept that they appear here so that I can have an opportunity whether the person is a male or a female, whether he is a foreigner or a national of my country, whether he was a member of UNPROFOR, et cetera. Glory be to all of those who lost their lives and appeared before the God, but I am not accepting any written statements. The only evidence that I accept is something that is to be said here in the courtroom, whether it being complimentary or whether it be criticism of myself. So I would like to hear everyone, Croats, Muslims, Albanians, because throughout the whole of my life, I worked with soldiers from across Yugoslavia, from Slovenia to Macedonia. I spent 30 years as a commander in Macedonia. You can find an enormous number of people who know me, just like the medical team knows everything about me, the team at that scanned me from head to toe. Now, let me draw a parallel here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me briefly respond to what you just said. I do understand that you would wish every witness to appear before this Court. Now, to what extent that will happen depends on various matters. The parties will present their case in the way they deem it fit to present their case. Now, if a party suggests that we could do on a certain matter with a written statement, then that party proposes to receive that evidence in the form of a written statement, then the other party will respond to that request, and finally the Chamber will decide, first of all, whether such a written statement will be accepted or not, and second, whether even if the evidence is presented in the form of a written statement, whether that witness still has to appear for cross-examination, to be cross-examined by the other party. These rules apply both to the Prosecution and to the Defence. I think it's clear on the record that you would wish every piece of evidence to -- introduced through viva voce evidence. Could you please move on to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, what is viva voce? Oh, it means live. Okay. Now, on to another topic. The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is no longer. The FRY also doesn't exist any more. The Commonwealth of Serbia and Montenegro doesn't exist any more. All the burden lies now on Serbia and the Serbian people and Republika Srpska and us, Serb detainees. It's one and the same people and it's one and the same land only divided by the River Drina. What I might object when it comes to Mr. Lukic, that he's using the term the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, what is that? That does not exist. If he had said the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina that would be all right in line with the Dayton Accords. The Prosecutor's office of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not exist. There may be a Prosecutor's office of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is a coalition of Croats, Herzegovinians and Muslims. This is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again interrupt you. If you are not happy with the terminology used by Mr. Lukic, please discuss it with him. It's not a matter for the Chamber at this moment to deal with. Could you please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was those gentlemen who first used the term the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. War crime against peace was committed against the SFRY, but I'll leave it at that. I will come back to this issue when the time comes. Now, I'm wondering why we, the detainees from Republika Srpska such as myself, don't have an opportunity to be visited by officials from Republika Srpska. Truth to tell, some people are coming from Serbia, and I'm referring to Consul Brkic. This is our country. This is our land. We are one people. And, therefore, I would kindly ask for permission for visits to be paid by the officials who are in power in Republika Srpska at the moment, because in my eyes that is a proper state. Following the Dayton agreement, no matter how much I participated in the creation of Republika Srpska, I am not requesting or demanding anything. Let them just come over and visit me. I learned from the media that they are at each other's throats. I was watching on Hayat TV that there was a group of Serb fighters, another group of Muslim fighters, and a third group of Croat fighters, and they went on strike against everyone. Now, if this gentleman is seeking evidence, why doesn't he call Divjak from Belgrade? He's an expert. I want to question him. He killed officers, JNA officers, on Dobrovoljacka street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you invited me to interrupt you when you raised your voice. That's what I'm doing at this moment. You started with a matter which is appropriately raised during a Status Conference, that is that you have some difficulties with the -- who is allowed to visit you, yes or no. Now, that is a matter which is not within the competence of the Chamber. It has no direct impact on the proceedings. Nevertheless, it's hereby on the record, and this means that the Registrar who is responsible for the UN Detention Unit, that you may address him on the matter. Mr. Lukic knows how to do it. It may be a complicated matter in terms of statehood or not. I totally stay out of that. Your request and your wish is clearly on the record and will be considered by those competent to deal with it. Next subject, please. May I remind you that we are at about the 20 minutes, so if you would please try to finish within the next five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five minutes. Thank you. I'm grateful for the six minutes as well. What I'm interested in is freedom and peace. I don't want you to give me freedom. I want to fight for it, because I would like to go and live in Belgrade, the capital of the Serbian nation, as a free man. I would like to go back to my wife, my son, my daughter-in-law, and my grandchildren, even if I have to go and live on the alms. I don't want any humanitarian aid provided to me by the US embassy, just like those villains who brought me here. And now I'm publicly demanding that the US General Wesley Clark be summoned here to testify against or for me. Never mind. He was in at least 14 states and at least 16 wars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You invited me to interrupt you when you raised your voice. I do it again. You are now entering again the matter of who should appear on whoever's behalf as witnesses before this Court. That is a matter which is not appropriately raised in a Status Conference. Would you please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since I have four minutes left, let me ask you this: Do I have the right at a Status Conference to be at least present when Mr. Groome and Mr. McCloskey are discussing issues with my Defence lawyers? I would like to clarify some things for them and save them effort of travelling to Macedonia or wherever. They don't need to investigate whether I attended that wedding. I attended hundreds of weddings in my life. And with this I would like to finish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladic. You -- if you give me one second. Mr. Mladic, the type of meetings which are held prior to this Status Conference are called Rule 65 ter meetings. It is mainly a meeting between the parties. They are often called and organised by the senior legal officers, or it's not even necessary that one of the Judges is present, although I thought it wise to attend those meetings, and the Rules specifically say that: "The presence of the accused is not necessary for meetings convened by the senior legal officer." And these are what we call the 65 ter meetings. Now, if there is any matter which you would like to be introduced at such a 65 ter meeting, you of course can instruct Mr. Lukic to raise these matters, and we heard today that some of the matters that are of your concerns were actually raised by Mr. Lukic. If there is any matter that you feel uncomfortable to have them discussed in your absence, you could ask Mr. Lukic to tell those present at the 65 ter meeting that he would prefer to deal with a certain matter during the Status Conference in your presence, and I take it he'll then discuss it with you and ultimately will take care that final discussions are not held between the parties without you knowing about it or without you being present during such discussions. This is a short, perhaps rather technical answer to your -- to your observations. Mr. Mladic, you said that is what you wished to say and to finish with. Thank you for your comments. If there's no other matter to be raised, I would adjourn, and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One minute, Mr. Mladic, on a matter appropriately raised during a Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you explained this nicely to me, I would like to improve my relationship with this Court, with all people involved. In the future, I'm going to rise when you enter, I will bow, and I will sit down when you tell me. Not because I respect you so much, but because I would like to take part in this as an accused, and I would like to do that in a fair manner. All you're going to get from me is the truth and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladic. It did not remain unnoticed when I entered the courtroom that everyone rising, you did not. I did not comment on it. I left it entirely to you, but it's highly appreciated that you say that you will join all the others in standing when the Judges enter the courtroom. It's appreciated. We adjourn, and I have to -- the next Status Conference will take place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn until the 24th of April, the next Status Conference, time and courtroom to be specified by the Registry at a later stage. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 5.49 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of April, 2012. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
